title: ANY TIPS FOR USING CLAUDE MCP (FIRST TIME GAMEDEV)
author: That-Ad111
selftext:
Hello. We are a team of BSIT 3rd year students and we are making a 2d pixel art sidescroller godot game as one of our major school projects. It is an adventure game where you would need to learn and use code to progress. We have all the assets we need and I have no Idea where to start. We will use Claude AI for creating the game. So my question is this:

\- How sould we use Claude efficiently?  
\- Can claude make scenes for the player, enemy, npcs, etc from scratch? Can I just tell claude which assets are which?  
\- On a scale of 1-10, how difficult would developing this game be for first time game developers?  
\- Do you have any tips or advise on how we should do this?

Any help would be greatly appreciated. Thanks!

comments.author: forgingtheflow
comments.body:
I don’t believe Claude has native image gen capability like ChatGPT, but you can connect Claude to something like seedream or another image gen ai. I use Astra 6.1 medium or high for artwork and opus 5.5 ultracode for coding. When ChatGPT has created something I ask it for a handover doc to give to the coding session (Claude) to wire it up.   
Like wise if I need artwork, I get the coding session to create a handover/instruction guide for the art/modelling session (ChatGPT) it’ll be a description and have the relevant details on what needs to be created so it should be simple for Claude to wire it into the game. You can likely get away with lower effort levels but they’ve worked well for me.   
So you can use Claude to plan and design the artwork then have something else create it. 

That’s of course one of many methods available.

comments.author: hubert-putu
comments.body:
On my experience, we need to have the "blueprint" of how the game will look like. Give the Claude some references and some specs, so it would not give you random results. From the scale 1-10 for beginner, i would give it 5. Godot is a solid choice imo, it's free and lightweight. 

Always start with specs, ask the Claude to generate technical, UI/Screens, constraint, art, assets, architecture, data model, analytics etc. Those kind of specs will help your project grow within your consent. Review all the specs carefully, make sure nothing out of scope. In this planning phase, i would use the Fable with at least on extra effort.

During the execution phase, i would just let the Claude create me the phases of working plan based on the specs, so it can be executed step by step, with test cases. I would choose the Opus 5.5 models, to safe some tokens.

comments.author: aura-32
comments.body:
Difficulty is maybe a 6/10 if you keep scope small. A few tips:

- Start with a one-page design doc (core loop, controls, 3 levels max) and give it to Claude at the start of every session.
- Yes, it can build scenes from scratch. Give it the folder layout and tell it which files are the player, enemies and tiles. It works best one scene at a time: player movement first, test it, then enemies.
- Use git and commit after every working step so you can roll back.
- For a team, have one person own the main scene and merge, or you'll fight over .tscn conflicts.
- Since your game teaches code, build that puzzle system early. It's the riskiest part.

comments.author: The_Toolsmith
comments.body:
>It also helped that I had built a 30 page game doc with what was in the game, lore, and mechanics I wanted.

THIS is likely the bit that makes the difference.  Spec, spec and spec again before writing a single line of code was the mantra when we were tackling any piece of software dev project.

We had the user manual 90% \_done\_ before initialising the github/svn/cvs/rcs for the first commit.  If you have a very clear direction in your head and in your spec and in your docs, then Claude can work magic off that.
